claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native, as-formed Fe-oxide surface film.
The native Fe-oxide film provides effective barrier protection to Q235 steel at room temperature.
At room temperature, the native Fe-oxide film self-heals minor defects.
The native Fe-oxide film becomes unstable during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Thermal-expansion mismatch generates stresses that cause the oxide film to crack or spall at high temperature.
Accelerated diffusion at elevated temperature contributes to oxide-film instability.
Cracking or spallation exposes fresh Q235 steel and thereby accelerates corrosion.
Annealing can modify a metallic surface or coating microstructure through thermal diffusion.
Annealing Q235 steel briefly at approximately 700 °C under inert atmosphere will modify its surface oxide.
Pre-annealing Q235 steel will produce a denser and more adherent Fe-oxide scale.
A denser, more adherent scale will be less susceptible to thermal-expansion mismatch and will retain protection during high-temperature salt exposure.
Both untreated and pre-annealed Q235 steel will exhibit low corrosion rates in room-temperature 3.5% NaCl.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, pre-annealed Q235 steel will have lower mass loss than untreated Q235 steel.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, pre-annealed Q235 steel will have fewer and smaller corrosion pits than untreated Q235 steel.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, pre-annealed Q235 steel will retain a more intact oxide layer than untreated Q235 steel.
Untreated Q235 steel will display significant oxide-scale spallation and accelerated corrosion during high-temperature salt exposure.
Corrosion mechanisms in Cr- or Mn-containing stainless steels and HEAs can differ from the proposed oxide-integrity mechanism for Q235 steel.
The proposed oxide-integrity mechanism should not govern conditions in which mechanical wear predominates over chemical corrosion.
